## B. Expanded findings

### 1. The 2020 event was a Bennu “touchdown,” which is probably the source of the mistake

NASA itself describes the Oct. 20, 2020 operation using language such as “touched down,” but the destination was **asteroid Bennu, more than 200 million miles from Earth**, not Earth. Even more precisely, NASA says the **round TAGSAM sampling head was the only part of OSIRIS-REx that contacted Bennu's surface**. Contact lasted roughly six seconds, after which a back-away maneuver carried the spacecraft clear. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="15"}

That makes “OSIRIS-REx landed in 2020” misleading even for Bennu. This was deliberately a **Touch-And-Go**, not a parked landing: descend, make momentary contact, collect regolith, and immediately retreat.

### 2. Collection and Earth delivery are separate milestones

The sample was collected on **Oct. 20, 2020**, but it remained aboard OSIRIS-REx for nearly three years. NASA's current FAQ reports the eventual returned bulk sample as **121.6 grams (4.29 oz)**. The sample was stowed in the return capsule on Oct. 28, and OSIRIS-REx did not begin its trip back toward Earth until May 10, 2021. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="16"}

The capsule itself did not separate until **Sept. 24, 2023**. NASA records release at 6:42 a.m. EDT while the parent spacecraft was about 63,000 miles from Earth. Four hours later the capsule entered the atmosphere and landed in Utah. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="17"}

### 3. What physically landed on Earth?

A purpose-built **Sample Return Capsule (SRC)** landed. It contained the sample canister and Bennu material and had its own heat shield and parachute system for atmospheric entry. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="18"}

The main OSIRIS-REx spacecraft remained in space. NASA's mission history explicitly says the capsule **“separated from the rest of the spacecraft and entered Earth's atmosphere”**, followed immediately by the clarification that the spacecraft itself **“didn't land back on Earth.”** :chatgpt-content-reference{index="19"}

That distinction is central: this was a **sample-return architecture**, not a spacecraft-return architecture.

### 4. “Continued unchanged to Apophis” is only partly true

There is a narrow sense in which continuity is real: OSIRIS-APEX is **the same surviving spacecraft**, not a newly launched replacement. NASA decided to reuse it because its instruments remained in good condition and it still had roughly a quarter of its fuel after returning the Bennu sample. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="20"}

But “unchanged” is incorrect in every mission-level sense that matters. The spacecraft:

- had **released and permanently lost its Sample Return Capsule**;
- executed a **diversion burn** so the spacecraft itself would miss Earth;
- switched from the completed Bennu sample-return mission to an **extended asteroid-rendezvous mission**;
- was renamed from **OSIRIS-REx** to **OSIRIS-APEX**;
- changed target from carbon-rich **Bennu** to stony **Apophis**;
- changed its principal science objective from collecting and returning a sample to studying how Earth's 2029 close encounter alters Apophis. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="21"}

NASA even describes the planned close approach to Apophis as repeating the Bennu maneuver **“minus sample collection”**: OSIRIS-APEX can use its thrusters to expose subsurface material, but it no longer has a return capsule waiting to bring another sample home. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="22"}

### 5. The rename was directly associated with the transition to the new mission

NASA's real-time mission update from Sept. 24, 2023 says that about 20 minutes after releasing the capsule, the spacecraft fired its engines toward its new mission to Apophis **“and was renamed OSIRIS-APEX.”** :chatgpt-content-reference{index="23"}

The expanded name is **Origins, Spectral Interpretation, Resource Identification and Security – Apophis Explorer**. NASA had already selected the extended mission before sample return; the post-delivery transition is when the operating spacecraft moved from the OSIRIS-REx primary mission to OSIRIS-APEX. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="24"}

## C. Questions you probably would have asked next

### “Did any part of the spacecraft touch a celestial body in 2020?”

Yes—but **Bennu**, not Earth, and only the TAGSAM collector head made surface contact during the sampling maneuver. NASA estimates the contact at approximately six seconds. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="25"}

### “Did OSIRIS-REx itself even enter Earth's atmosphere in 2023?”

No. Only the detached capsule was sent onto an atmospheric-entry trajectory. About 20 minutes after release, the mothership deliberately burned its engines to divert away from Earth. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="26"}

### “Was the capsule a separate spacecraft?”

It is better described as a **separable re-entry vehicle/component of OSIRIS-REx** rather than the entire interplanetary spacecraft. It had the hardware required to protect the sample during high-speed atmospheric entry and to land by parachute, but the main spacecraft supplied propulsion, navigation, power, and science operations throughout the interplanetary mission. NASA consistently calls it the **Sample Return Capsule**. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="27"}

### “Why send the old spacecraft to Apophis instead of ending the mission?”

NASA says OSIRIS-REx remained healthy and had about **one quarter of its fuel** remaining. NASA considered other possible destinations, including Venus and comets, before choosing Apophis. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="28"}

Apophis offers an unusual scientific opportunity because its April 13, 2029 Earth encounter will take it about **20,000 miles (32,000 km) above Earth's surface**, with Earth's gravity expected to alter its orbit and rotation and potentially modify its surface. OSIRIS-APEX is intended to study those changes afterward. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="29"}

## D. Important things you might not have known to ask

**The word “return” is itself potentially misleading.** NASA frequently says OSIRIS-REx “returned to Earth” on Sept. 24, 2023. In mission shorthand that means the spacecraft came back to Earth's vicinity and delivered its payload; it does **not** mean the spacecraft landed. NASA's detailed materials make the flyby-and-capsule-release architecture explicit. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="30"}

**The sample was not simply sitting loose in the re-entry capsule since October 20.** Sampling occurred on Oct. 20; NASA then accelerated stowage after images showed abundant material, and closed the Sample Return Capsule on Oct. 28. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="31"}

**OSIRIS-APEX is already an active mission, not merely a proposed future reuse.** NASA's current mission page lists it as active and gives Apophis as the destination. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="32"}

**Apophis is not a second sample-return mission.** The planned study includes mapping, spectroscopy, laser-altimeter observations, and a low-altitude thruster maneuver designed to uncover subsurface material, but NASA explicitly describes that operation as occurring without sample collection. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="33"}

## E. Contradictions and alternative explanations

There is a genuine **NASA-source discrepancy concerning the precise 2029 rendezvous month**.

A December 2023 NASA article, updated Jan. 2, 2024, says OSIRIS-APEX would arrive **later in April 2029**, after Apophis' April 13 Earth encounter. A February 2024 mission update likewise said it was heading toward an April 2029 rendezvous. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="34"}

However, NASA's **current dedicated OSIRIS-APEX mission page** now lists:

> Rendezvous date: **June 2029**

and NASA's current Apophis exploration page likewise says it will arrive at Apophis **in June** for an 18-month campaign. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="35"}

Those claims should not be silently merged. The stronger current formulation is therefore: **OSIRIS-APEX will rendezvous with Apophis after its April 13, 2029 Earth encounter; NASA's current mission page specifies June 2029.** The older April date appears to reflect an earlier mission timeline.

There is another, less consequential example of evolving information. Immediately after landing, NASA pages described an **estimated ~250 g** sample based on pre-opening estimates. Once curation was complete enough for an official measurement, NASA announced the returned bulk sample mass as **121.6 g** in February 2024. That is not evidence of different collections; it is a preliminary estimate superseded by a measured value. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="36"}

The erroneous timeline itself therefore has a plausible non-exotic explanation: somebody may have combined the phrase **“touchdown” in October 2020** with later descriptions saying the mission “returned to Earth,” while omitting the crucial distinction between Bennu TAG, capsule return, and mothership flyby.

## F. Remaining uncertainties

The basic chronology is not materially uncertain: NASA's mission history, contemporaneous TAG reports, capsule-return coverage, FAQ, and current OSIRIS-APEX page all agree on the central sequence.

The main live uncertainty relevant here is the **future 2029 operational timeline**. June 2029 is NASA's current published rendezvous date, but interplanetary mission schedules and trajectories can change before encounter. What can be established robustly now is that the target is Apophis and that the rendezvous is planned **after its April 13, 2029 close Earth passage**. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="37"}

There is also a semantic rather than factual uncertainty around when one says OSIRIS-REx “became” OSIRIS-APEX. NASA had approved and named the extended mission before the sample-return event, while contemporaneous Sept. 24, 2023 operations reporting describes the spacecraft as being renamed following its divert maneuver. That distinction does not affect what physically occurred. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="38"}

Very little could overturn the principal correction because it is directly documented by multiple NASA records. To change it, one would need credible mission telemetry or NASA documentation showing either that the main spacecraft entered Earth's atmosphere in 2023 or that an Earth landing occurred in 2020. NIST's migration work explicitly emphasizes interoperability and vendor implementations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"} |
| **Days 21–26** | Run one **staging/lab** experiment at the easiest boundary. Prefer a vendor-supported TLS path using ML-KEM or, if TLS support is unavailable, a signing/verifying proof of concept with ML-DSA using a maintained implementation. Measure handshake/signature size, latency, CPU, failure behavior and legacy-client compatibility. | Test results, not a production migration. |
| **Days 27–30** | Convert findings into a migration backlog: systems, blocking vendor, target PQC primitive, prerequisite upgrade, test requirement, rollback method and priority. Also record whether components are cryptographically agile enough to change algorithms again. | A 90-day/12-month roadmap with the first implementable migration item. NIST's current crypto-agility guidance emphasizes being able to replace algorithms while preserving interoperability and operations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"} |

With only one engineer, I would **not spend this month writing an ML-KEM or ML-DSA implementation**. The scarce engineering time is better spent determining which existing libraries, TLS terminators, PKI components, HSMs and update verifiers can consume standardized implementations safely.

### Inventory fields with the highest information value

The inventory does not need to be enterprise-scale. For each crypto use, capture: the business/data purpose; confidentiality versus authentication/signature role; current RSA/ECC/DH/etc. algorithm; protocol such as TLS/code signing; data retention/confidentiality lifetime; certificate and key lifetime; TLS termination point; crypto library/runtime version; CDN/load-balancer/KMS/HSM/CA vendor; server and client/verifier populations; whether the algorithm is configurable without rebuilding the product; and the dependency that would block changing it.

That follows NIST's definition of a cryptographic inventory, which includes algorithms, protocols/services, keys and lifecycle metadata, certificate chains, dependent components, and data protected by the cryptography. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"}

### Questions worth sending vendors

| Vendor area | Questions that materially change your plan |
|---|---|
| **TLS/CDN/load balancer/cloud** | “Do you support NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM for customer-facing TLS today? In which product/version and protocol mechanism? Is deployment hybrid/combined with classical key establishment, and what exact client support is required? What happens when a peer lacks support? Can we see negotiated-algorithm telemetry and disable/roll back the feature?” |
| **TLS/PKI certificates** | “What is your roadmap for PQC authentication/signatures? Do you support FIPS 204 ML-DSA or FIPS 205 SLH-DSA in the certificate/tooling path? Which browsers, TLS libraries, proxies and certificate formats interoperate with it?” |
| **HSM/KMS/signing service** | “Can the service generate and protect ML-DSA signing keys and perform FIPS 204 signing? Is SLH-DSA supported? Is support GA, preview or roadmap? If we require validated cryptographic modules, what is the relevant validation status?” |
| **Update framework/runtime/device client** | “Can the existing package/update format represent and verify ML-DSA signatures? Which deployed client versions can verify them? Can signature formats be versioned or multiple signatures carried during transition? Are there size limits or bootloader/agent constraints?” |
| **All critical vendors** | “What upgrade is required, when does the supported version become available, what are the interoperability limitations, and what rollback path exists?” |

For update signing specifically, **verifier support is at least as important as signer support**: being able to produce an ML-DSA signature does little good if a substantial installed client population cannot parse or verify it.

### How I would prioritize this company

The **20-year customer-record lifetime raises the priority of confidentiality/key-establishment discovery**. TLS traffic that can be captured today could matter long after the session itself ends if the underlying customer data remains sensitive; NIST explicitly includes long-lived data in the quantum-readiness inventory and describes TLS as an important target for post-quantum protection. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

Software-update signing is also important, but its risk shape is different: the concern is future ability to forge signatures accepted by verifiers rather than decrypt previously captured traffic. Start its migration work now by inventorying signing keys, formats, HSM/KMS dependencies and every verifier population, with **ML-DSA/FIPS 204 as the first standardized candidate to investigate** and SLH-DSA/FIPS 205 retained as the standardized alternative. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="11"}

I would therefore define the **day-30 success criterion** as: *complete crypto inventory + long-lived-data priority map + vendor readiness matrix + one interoperability proof + prioritized migration backlog*. A production-wide PQC cutover is not a credible 30-day success criterion for one engineer unless your existing vendors already make it essentially a configuration change.

Finally, there is **no basis here for assigning this SaaS a universal mandatory deployment date**. NIST says organizations should begin migration, and its transition material discusses deprecation timelines for quantum-vulnerable algorithms, but government requirements and NIST standards-transition dates should not automatically be converted into a private company's compliance deadline without knowing its jurisdiction, customers, contracts and regulatory scope. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="12"}

Given a 20-year data-retention horizon and only one engineer this quarter, the first 30 days should be an **inventory-and-dependency sprint, not a production cryptography rewrite**. NIST’s migration work explicitly emphasizes discovering where vulnerable public-key cryptography is used, building a cryptographic inventory, and then prioritizing migration based on risk. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

### What maps to what

| Your use case | NIST standard | Algorithm | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS key establishment | **FIPS 203** | **ML-KEM** | Establishes a shared secret over a public channel; it is not a bulk-data cipher. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"} |
| Software-update signatures | **FIPS 204** | **ML-DSA** | Post-quantum digital signatures; NIST describes it as its primary general-purpose PQ signature standard. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"} |
| Alternative signature path | **FIPS 205** | **SLH-DSA** | Hash-based post-quantum signatures using a substantially different construction; NIST describes it as a backup alternative to ML-DSA. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"} |

All three final FIPS were published on **August 13, 2024**. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

The distinction matters: replacing ECDH/RSA-style key establishment in a TLS stack points toward **ML-KEM/FIPS 203**. Replacing RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA-style signatures on update artifacts points toward **ML-DSA or SLH-DSA**, not ML-KEM.

### A realistic first 30 days

NIST defines a useful inventory broadly: algorithms, protocols, keys and their metadata, certificates, applications, libraries, HSMs, dependencies, and the data being protected—without recording secret key material. It specifically calls out long-lived sensitive data because of “harvest now, decrypt later.” :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

For a one-engineer team, a spreadsheet or small repository file is enough. The goal is coverage, not a new asset-management platform.

**Days 6–10 — Trace the two real trust chains.** For TLS, diagram something like `client → CDN/WAF → load balancer → app → database/API`, marking each point that establishes an asymmetric session. For update signing, trace `build → signing service/HSM → artifact → repository/CDN → updater/package manager → verifier`. The critical question is not merely whether your signer can generate ML-DSA signatures, but whether **every verifier that must accept an update can understand them**.

Also inventory encryption protecting the 20-year records **at rest**. FIPS 203 solves key establishment; simply adopting ML-KEM for TLS does not automatically migrate database encryption, backups, archived wrapped keys, or old ciphertext.

**Days 11–15 — Ask vendors for concrete PQC capabilities and dates.** This is likely the highest-leverage work the engineer can perform. NIST’s migration project explicitly treats vendor/product interoperability as a central migration problem, including internet protocols, certificates, digital trust, and HSMs. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

Ask your TLS/CDN/cloud/crypto-library/KMS/HSM and signing-tool vendors:

- Do you support **FIPS 203 ML-KEM**, and in which product/version/API?
- How is it integrated into TLS or other relevant protocols, and what client/server compatibility requirements exist?
- Is there a migration or compatibility mode for peers that do not yet support PQC?
- Which certificates, CAs, proxies, gateways, or TLS inspection products block deployment?
- Do you support **FIPS 204 ML-DSA** and/or **FIPS 205 SLH-DSA** for signing and verification?
- Can your HSM/KMS generate and protect those keys, rotate them, back them up where appropriate, and expose the needed signing APIs?
- Which code-signing formats, artifact registries, package managers, operating systems, bootloaders, or update agents can verify those signatures today?
- What are the key/signature/certificate size and latency impacts?
- What is the rollback/fallback mechanism if interoperability fails?
- If you require FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, what is the relevant validation status rather than merely “algorithm supported”?

NIST already has algorithm-validation support for ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, but product/module validation requirements are a separate question from an algorithm appearing in a FIPS. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}

**Days 16–22 — Run one bounded lab experiment.** Do not write a PQ implementation yourself. Pick the closest supported staging path from an existing TLS/provider stack and measure handshake success, compatibility, latency, CPU/memory, and failure behavior. NIST’s NCCoE specifically emphasizes controlled interoperability and performance testing before deployment. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"}

Separately, create a test artifact signed with the vendor-supported PQ signature option and verify it through as much of the real update chain as possible. For your initial target, **ML-DSA/FIPS 204 is the natural first signature candidate** because NIST identifies it as the primary signature standard; keep SLH-DSA/FIPS 205 in the design as an alternative with mathematical diversity rather than trying to deploy both immediately. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"}

**Days 23–30 — Produce a migration backlog, not a “PQC complete” claim.** Classify every item as `ready now`, `vendor upgrade available`, `vendor roadmap`, `protocol/ecosystem blocked`, or `unknown`. Give the highest priority to long-lived confidential information crossing quantum-vulnerable public-key sessions, externally exposed TLS endpoints, high-value signing keys, and dependencies with long upgrade cycles.

Add crypto agility requirements to future purchases and development: algorithms should not be hard-coded across the application, and protocol/library/provider changes should be replaceable without redesigning the service. NIST's current crypto-agility guidance defines precisely this ability to replace cryptography while preserving security and operations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

### What I would expect at day 30

The useful deliverable is about four pages plus the inventory: a map of your TLS and software-signing cryptography; a list of quantum-vulnerable RSA/ECC dependencies; a vendor support matrix for ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA; results from one or two staging experiments; and a prioritized backlog with blockers and owners.

For this SaaS, I would put **TLS/key-establishment discovery first** because the records have a 20-year confidentiality requirement. Traffic intercepted today can remain valuable long enough for a future cryptanalytic capability to matter; NIST specifically identifies TLS as exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later concerns. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="11"} The software-update signature path should be inventoried in the same month, but its migration pressure is different: the concern is future forgery/authenticity rather than decrypting traffic captured today.

There is deliberately **no company-specific “must be finished by year X” date here**. NIST says organizations should begin migrating now, and its draft IR 8547 lays out a transition direction for NIST standards, but IR 8547 remains an **Initial Public Draft** as of September 2026. Its dates should not be converted into an invented universal compliance deadline for an arbitrary SaaS company. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="12"}

## Direct answer

For this SaaS, the first 30 days should be a **discovery-and-readiness sprint, not a wholesale cryptographic replacement project**. With one engineer, the highest-value outcome is a reliable cryptographic inventory, a risk-ranked migration map, concrete answers from your TLS/signing vendors, and—only where the existing stack supports it—a small staging test.

The standards map cleanly:

| Use case | NIST standard | What it does | Relevance here |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS/key establishment | **FIPS 203 — ML-KEM** | Establishes a shared secret over a public channel | The PQC primitive relevant to protecting TLS session-key establishment against future quantum attack. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"} |
| Software-update signatures | **FIPS 204 — ML-DSA** | Post-quantum digital signatures | NIST describes ML-DSA as its primary general-purpose PQ signature standard. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"} |
| Alternative signature scheme | **FIPS 205 — SLH-DSA** | Stateless hash-based digital signatures | Also standardized for signatures; NIST describes it as a mathematically different backup alternative to ML-DSA. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"} |

The 20-year lifetime of your customer records makes the **TLS/key-establishment path the first risk to characterize**. NIST specifically distinguishes confidentiality from authentication: intercepted encrypted traffic can be retained for later decryption, so the lifetime of sensitive information affects key-establishment migration urgency. Digital-signature/authentication risk follows a different timeline. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

Do **not** interpret this as “replace TLS with raw ML-KEM” or “rewrite the signing system around ML-DSA this month.” PQC has to be incorporated into actual protocols, libraries, PKI, KMS/HSMs, clients, update formats, and vendor products; NIST explicitly treats interoperability and migration as system-level problems. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

### Working brief

Your immediate goal is to reduce uncertainty enough to produce an implementable roadmap. The hard constraint is one engineer this quarter. A successful first month therefore means you can answer: where quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography exists, which uses protect long-lived confidentiality, which vendors control each migration point, whether those vendors have supported PQC paths, and what can safely be tested next.

The biggest unresolved facts are where TLS actually terminates—CDN, cloud load balancer, API gateway, application server, service mesh, or some combination—and how your software-update verification chain works. Those facts could materially reorder the later implementation work.

### Prioritized question tree

| Priority | Question | Current conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Where is quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography actually used? | Build the inventory first. NIST's NCCoE says organizations cannot effectively prioritize cryptography they have not identified. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"} |
| 2 | Which uses expose 20-year-sensitive information? | TLS carrying those records deserves early attention because of harvest-now/decrypt-later risk. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"} |
| 3 | Who controls each cryptographic boundary? | This determines whether you migrate code or wait for/configure a CDN, cloud, TLS library, CA, KMS/HSM, or signing platform. |
| 4 | Can the TLS ecosystem support PQ key establishment interoperably? | Evaluate vendor-supported ML-KEM or standards-based hybrid mechanisms rather than inventing a protocol. NIST's migration draft explicitly anticipates classical/PQC hybrid approaches. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"} |
| 5 | Can every software-update verifier understand a future PQ signature? | This is critical. NIST highlights devices whose verification code may be difficult or impossible to update as a special code-signing migration risk. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"} |
| 6 | How easily can algorithms be changed again? | Treat crypto agility as an architectural requirement, not just a one-time PQC conversion. NIST defines crypto agility as the ability to replace/adapt algorithms while maintaining security and operations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"} |

## A realistic first 30 days

1. **Days 1–5 — Create the inventory and scope.** Make one spreadsheet or small repository-backed inventory. Record every known TLS endpoint and signing operation, including protocol, current asymmetric algorithm, cryptographic library/service, termination point, certificate or key owner, vendor, environments, data carried, retention/sensitivity, external clients, and upgrade owner. Do not store private-key material in the inventory. Include hidden dependencies such as CDN TLS, load balancers, service-to-service TLS, database connections, VPN/SSH if relevant, KMS/HSMs, package-signing services, timestamping services, CAs, and CI/CD signing steps. NIST defines a useful inventory broadly enough to include algorithms, protocols, keys and their metadata, certificates, systems, data flows, and long-lived sensitive data. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

2. **Days 6–10 — Trace the TLS path end to end.** Determine exactly where a customer's connection is decrypted and re-encrypted. Record every independent key-establishment hop. Mark paths carrying customer records with long confidentiality requirements. The important distinction is that FIPS 203 specifies **ML-KEM**, a KEM for establishing shared secrets; it is not itself a drop-in TLS implementation. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="11"}

3. **Days 11–15 — Map the software-update trust chain.** Record the current signing algorithm, where the private signing key resides, which service/HSM/KMS performs signing, package/update formats, public-key distribution mechanism, trust anchors, verifier implementations, supported client versions, and how long old clients remain in service. Determine whether verifiers can be upgraded before you change the signer. For this use case, evaluate **ML-DSA/FIPS 204** first; retain **SLH-DSA/FIPS 205** as a standardized alternative that may matter for diversity or platform-specific requirements. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="12"}

4. **Days 16–20 — Send focused questions to every critical provider.** Do this for the CDN/load balancer/cloud provider, TLS library/runtime, CA, signing service, KMS/HSM, package/update ecosystem, and any client platform you do not control. Get written roadmap answers rather than assuming that algorithm support in a library means end-to-end product support. NIST's migration work explicitly covers libraries, hardware, PKI infrastructure, applications, services, compatibility, and interoperability. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="13"}

5. **Days 21–25 — Produce a risk-ranked migration map.** Put the long-lived-data TLS paths at the top; then identify signing/verifier combinations where clients could remain deployed for many years or cannot easily be upgraded. Separate “we control this” from “vendor dependency,” and distinguish “available now,” “available experimentally,” “roadmapped,” and “unknown.” Do not assign a deployment date based merely on a predicted quantum-computer date.

6. **Days 26–30 — Run one bounded staging experiment and publish the next-quarter plan.** If one of your existing TLS providers already has a supported PQ or hybrid ML-KEM configuration, test it in staging against representative clients. Measure compatibility, handshake failures, latency, bandwidth/message-size effects, fallback behavior, observability, and rollback. If no supported path exists, do **not** spend the month implementing a custom KEM handshake; use the time to close vendor gaps and document migration triggers. End the month with owners, dependencies, test criteria, and a 60–90 day backlog.

### The inventory that will actually be useful

A minimal row should contain roughly these fields:

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| System/service and environment | Locates the dependency |
| Cryptographic purpose | Key establishment, signature, authentication, key wrapping, etc. |
| Protocol/format | TLS, update manifest, package signature, certificate, etc. |
| Current algorithm | Reveals quantum-vulnerable public-key use |
| Crypto library/provider | Tells you where migration capability must appear |
| Key/certificate owner and lifecycle | Exposes operational dependencies |
| TLS/signature termination point | Separates your code from vendor-managed crypto |
| Data protected and sensitivity lifetime | Drives HNDL prioritization |
| Client/verifier population | Identifies interoperability risk |
| Vendor/product/version | Makes roadmap questions actionable |
| PQC status | None / roadmap / experimental / production-supported |
| Upgrade and rollback path | Tests crypto agility |
| Blocking dependency and owner | Converts inventory into a migration plan |

NIST's current migration FAQ specifically recommends starting with cryptographic asset discovery and inventory, and its NCCoE project has separate workstreams for cryptographic visibility/risk management and interoperability. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="14"}

### Vendor questions worth asking

Rather than “Do you support quantum-safe crypto?”, ask questions that can produce an engineering decision:

| Vendor question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Do you support **FIPS 203 ML-KEM** in the exact TLS/product path we use? | Algorithm-library support alone is insufficient |
| Is the implementation production-supported, preview, or experimental? | Determines deployment risk |
| Which protocol mechanism or hybrid construction is used? | Prevents treating raw ML-KEM as a complete TLS design |
| Which server and client versions interoperate with it? | Exposes compatibility gaps |
| What happens when the peer lacks PQC support? | Identifies fallback/downgrade behavior |
| What telemetry tells us whether PQC/hybrid negotiation actually occurred? | Needed for staged rollout |
| What performance or packet-size impacts should we test? | PQ algorithms can change operational characteristics |
| For signing, when will you support **ML-DSA/FIPS 204** and, if relevant, **SLH-DSA/FIPS 205**? | Maps the signing roadmap |
| Can our current HSM/KMS protect and operate those signing keys? | Hardware/API support may be the blocker |
| Can the update/package format carry classical and PQ signatures during transition? | May enable an interoperability period |
| Can old verifiers be upgraded before a PQ-only signature becomes necessary? | Critical code-signing dependency |
| If FIPS validation matters to us, what validated module/product version will provide this support? | “Implements the algorithm” and “validated deployment” are different claims |
| What is your migration and rollback procedure? | Measures practical crypto agility |

### Evidence and why the priorities differ

NIST finalized all three initial standards on **August 13, 2024**. FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM for shared-secret establishment; FIPS 204 defines ML-DSA signatures; and FIPS 205 defines SLH-DSA signatures. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="15"}

The important reasoning for this SaaS is not merely “20 years is a long time.” NIST says data can be collected while protected by today's public-key key establishment and decrypted later if a sufficiently capable quantum computer becomes available. Its transition draft therefore says the HNDL threat should influence the migration timeline for network-protocol key establishment. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="16"} That makes TLS paths carrying your long-lived customer information a rational first priority.

Software-update signing is different. An attacker cannot generally store a past authentication event and later retroactively forge it in the same manner as stored ciphertext. But NIST flags a separate issue: code verifiers that cannot be updated may need quantum-resistant verification capability while they are still deployable. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="17"} So the highest-value question is **how long your update-verifying clients live and whether their trust code can be upgraded**.

### Material assumptions and alternatives

This plan assumes that the records' contents actually traverse the TLS connections you operate, that you are not already using a managed PQ-capable edge, and that there is no regulatory or contractual deadline omitted from the case. It also assumes the software-update clients can potentially be changed; an immutable verifier would increase signing urgency substantially.

A credible alternative would be to deploy vendor-supported PQ/hybrid TLS immediately if your entire relevant client population already supports it. Another would be to defer any production cryptographic change this quarter and concentrate solely on inventory/vendor readiness if compatibility is uncertain. With one engineer, either can be sensible; implementing your own new TLS or signature protocol generally is not the useful first move.

There is also no reason from the facts supplied to replace all symmetric encryption merely because you are starting PQC migration. Your concrete problem here is the quantum vulnerability of **public-key** key establishment and signatures.

### Remaining uncertainty and deadlines

NIST's current posture is to encourage organizations to begin migration and inventory work now. Its NCCoE guidance emphasizes discovery, prioritization, vendor coordination, and interoperability. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="18"}

That is **not a universal private-company deployment deadline**. In fact, NIST's current publication page still identifies IR 8547, the detailed transition-timeline document, as an **Initial Public Draft**; NIST's FAQ separately identifies a mandate for U.S. federal agencies rather than describing one universal mandate for all organizations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="19"} Your actual deployment dates should therefore come from data-lifetime risk, customer/regulatory obligations, client lifetime, vendor readiness, and testing—not from inventing a fixed quantum-computer date.

One current implementation detail also argues for using maintained vendor/library implementations rather than coding directly from the specifications: NIST's FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 pages currently carry notices about potential errata/updates. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="20"}

## Direct answer

For this SaaS, the first 30 days should be a **risk-driven discovery and migration-planning sprint, not a production crypto rewrite**. With one engineer, the highest-value outcome is to know exactly where quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography protects the 20-year records, establish what your TLS and signing vendors can support, and run one or two controlled compatibility experiments.

The standards map cleanly:

| Function | NIST standard | Algorithm | Application here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Establishing secret keys for encrypted communications | **FIPS 203** | **ML-KEM** | Relevant to the key-establishment side of TLS migration |
| Digital signatures | **FIPS 204** | **ML-DSA** | Primary PQC candidate for signing software updates |
| Digital signatures, different construction | **FIPS 205** | **SLH-DSA** | Alternative/backup signature approach; NIST describes it as based on different mathematics |

FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM specifically as a mechanism for establishing a shared secret over a public channel; it is **not itself the bulk-data encryption algorithm**. FIPS 204 defines ML-DSA for generating and verifying digital signatures. FIPS 205 defines the hash-based SLH-DSA signature scheme; NIST has characterized ML-DSA as its primary general signature standard and SLH-DSA as an alternative based on different mathematics. All three final standards were published August 13, 2024. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

Because your records must remain confidential for **20 years**, discovery of the TLS paths carrying those records deserves especially high priority. NIST/CISA/NSA explicitly identify long secrecy lifetimes and “harvest now, decrypt later” as reasons to start planning early. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}

### A realistic first 30 days

1. **Days 1–5 — Build a small crypto inventory, starting with the 20-year data path.** Trace one representative customer record from browser/API client through CDN/WAF/load balancer, TLS termination, application services, databases, backups, exports, and external integrations. Record every place asymmetric cryptography appears: TLS versions and key-establishment algorithms, certificates and CA dependencies, API/service TLS, update-signing keys and algorithms, CI/CD signing libraries, KMS/HSM use, SSH/VPN if material, and third-party services. For each entry capture owner/vendor, algorithm, library/product, configuration location, whether you control it, data protected, required confidentiality/signature lifetime, and whether the component can be upgraded. NIST's migration guidance specifically recommends inventories covering network protocols, applications/libraries, software-update mechanisms, and CI/CD dependencies, correlated with the sensitivity and protection lifetime of the data. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

2. **Days 6–10 — Rank the inventory rather than trying to migrate everything.** Put externally observable TLS carrying the long-lived customer records in the first risk bucket. Separately flag update-signature verification points that may live for years—for example installed agents, appliances, desktop clients, bootloaders, or customers that update infrequently. Lower priority goes to easily replaceable internal components whose data has little long-term secrecy value. This is consistent with NIST's risk-based approach: inventory first, then use data criticality, protection lifetime, dependencies, and system characteristics to decide migration order. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

3. **Days 11–15 — Send focused questions to your critical vendors.** Start with whoever terminates public TLS, your cloud/load-balancer/CDN provider, TLS library/runtime supplier, CA/certificate tooling provider, and update-signing KMS/HSM or signing-service provider. Ask for supported PQC algorithms and protocol integrations—not merely whether the vendor is “quantum safe.” NIST specifically recommends asking vendors for their PQC roadmaps and even for lists of embedded cryptography that ordinary discovery tools may miss. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

4. **Days 16–22 — Run controlled experiments, not a bespoke implementation.** In a staging environment, determine whether your existing TLS stack or provider offers a standards-based/hybrid PQC-capable key-establishment mode and measure compatibility, handshake behavior, latency, observability, failure/fallback behavior, and client coverage. Separately determine whether your signing stack can generate, store, distribute, and verify ML-DSA signatures without changing production. Do not write your own ML-KEM or ML-DSA implementation; the practical question for a one-engineer SaaS is whether maintained libraries, protocols, KMS/HSMs, and vendors can carry the migration.

5. **Days 23–30 — Produce a migration backlog with explicit dependencies.** For every important crypto use, assign one of four states: *ready to pilot*, *blocked on vendor*, *requires application/protocol change*, or *needs more discovery*. Put owners and vendor dependencies beside each item. Your quarter-two work should emerge from this evidence rather than from a predetermined “replace RSA/ECDH everywhere” project. NIST's current crypto-agility guidance defines the broader objective as being able to replace or adapt algorithms while maintaining security and operations, which is a better design goal than merely hard-coding today's PQC choice. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

## The inventory that matters most

For a one-engineer team, I would keep the inventory to roughly these fields rather than buying a large cryptographic asset-management program immediately:

| Field | Why it changes your migration decision |
|---|---|
| System / endpoint / service | Identifies the migration unit |
| Cryptographic purpose | Key establishment, signature, certificate authentication, etc. |
| Current algorithm/protocol | Identifies quantum-vulnerable dependency |
| Library/product/vendor | Shows whether you or a supplier must fix it |
| Data/process protected | Links crypto to actual business risk |
| Protection lifetime | Critical for the 20-year-record problem |
| Internet exposure / capturability | Helps prioritize long-lived confidentiality |
| Key/certificate source | Finds KMS, HSM, CA and trust dependencies |
| Verifier lifetime | Critical for software-update signing |
| Upgrade mechanism | Reveals components that may become stranded |
| PQC/hybrid support today | Separates pilotable items from vendor blockers |
| Vendor/EOL date | Prevents building plans around products that will disappear |

This closely matches the kinds of characteristics NIST's migration project calls out: current algorithms, key/signature-size constraints, handshake protocols, crypto libraries, agility, software-update capability, suppliers, key/certificate sources, validation requirements, support lifetime, and information sensitivity. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

## Vendor questions worth asking

Rather than asking “Do you support post-quantum cryptography?”, send vendors questions specific enough to produce actionable answers:

| Area | Questions |
|---|---|
| TLS/CDN/load balancer | Which PQC or hybrid key-establishment mechanisms are supported today? Which use ML-KEM? On which TLS versions/products/regions? What client compatibility restrictions exist? Can rollout be enabled per hostname or percentage? Is fallback visible in telemetry? |
| Runtime/TLS library | Which released version supports standardized ML-KEM-based protocol integration? Is it production-supported? What upgrade or API changes are required? |
| Cloud provider | Which managed services terminate TLS on our behalf, and what is the PQC roadmap for each? Do we need configuration changes, application changes, or product replacement? |
| CA/certificate ecosystem | What PQC signature/certificate capabilities are planned, and what dependencies exist on browsers, clients, PKI profiles, or standards? |
| KMS/HSM/signing service | Do you support **ML-DSA/FIPS 204** key generation, protected key storage, signing and verification? What is the roadmap? Is SLH-DSA supported or planned? |
| Update framework | Can an update carry multiple signatures during transition? Can existing clients learn a new signature algorithm securely? Can the verifier itself be upgraded? |
| Every critical vendor | What quantum-vulnerable cryptography is embedded internally that customers cannot discover? What product versions will receive PQC support, and what are their support/EOL dates? |

The last question is important: NIST's quantum-readiness guidance explicitly warns that discovery tools may not find cryptography embedded inside commercial products and recommends obtaining that information from suppliers. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}

## Why TLS gets early attention

**Established fact:** NIST identifies long-lived confidentiality as a reason to prepare early because adversaries can retain encrypted material for later attacks. Your stated retention horizon is 20 years, so this consideration directly applies to at least some customer data if confidentiality is expected for a comparable period. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"}

**Strong inference:** your first engineering investigation should therefore follow the TLS/key-establishment paths by which that data enters, leaves, or moves between systems. The objective is not simply “does our website use TLS 1.3?” but **who actually performs key establishment at every boundary and whether that component has a credible ML-KEM migration path**.

There is an important boundary here: PQC does not imply replacing all symmetric encryption. FIPS 203 produces a shared secret that can subsequently be used with symmetric cryptography; the KEM and bulk-data encryption functions are distinct. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"}

## Why update signing is a separate problem

Your software-update chain should be inventoried concurrently, but it has a different failure mode. The central question is whether a future adversary could forge an update that a long-lived client would accept.

FIPS 204's ML-DSA is the natural first standardized signature mechanism to investigate. FIPS 205's SLH-DSA provides a standardized alternative based on a different construction. That does **not** mean you should immediately dual-sign everything with both; verifier compatibility, signature sizes, package formats, HSM support, trust-root management and your update architecture determine the practical migration. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

The expert blind spot is often the verifier rather than the signer. If an update verifier is baked into software or hardware that cannot itself be securely taught a new algorithm, a future signing-service upgrade will not solve the problem. That is why “can every deployed verifier be upgraded?” belongs near the top of the inventory.

## Working brief and question tree

Your working brief is: **protect data with a 20-year lifetime and preserve trustworthy software updates, with one engineer available this quarter and no evidence yet that the underlying cloud/TLS/signing vendors are PQC-ready.** Success in 30 days therefore means visibility, prioritization, vendor commitments and a tested migration path—not universal deployment.

The investigation branches that materially affect the next decision are:

| Priority | Question | Why it could change the roadmap |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Where is TLS actually terminated for the 20-year data? | Determines who owns ML-KEM migration |
| 1 | Which data really requires confidentiality for most of those 20 years? | Determines harvest-now/decrypt-later priority |
| 1 | Can deployed update verifiers be upgraded? | Could make signature migration urgent |
| 2 | Do TLS vendors already provide a supported PQC/hybrid path? | Could turn migration from engineering work into configuration/testing |
| 2 | Does the KMS/HSM support ML-DSA? | May block production signature migration |
| 2 | Can packages carry transitional multiple signatures? | Changes migration architecture |
| 3 | Are there regulatory/FIPS-validation requirements? | May constrain product/library choices |
| 3 | Which clients cannot support larger/new cryptographic messages? | Determines compatibility strategy |

## Alternatives and failure modes

The main alternative to this inventory-first approach is an immediate PQC deployment. For a one-engineer company that is usually a poor first use of the month: you may modify application code while the actual TLS cryptography is performed by a CDN, load balancer or managed service, or implement signatures that current clients cannot verify. NIST's migration work is explicitly organized around **cryptographic discovery followed by interoperability testing**, which supports inventory-first sequencing. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="11"}

The opposite failure is “wait until quantum computers arrive.” That ignores both migration lead time and the long-lived-data issue. NIST now says organizations should begin migrating and emphasizes finding vulnerable uses and planning their replacement. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="12"}

Another failure is to interpret a date such as **2035** as your company's universal deadline. NIST's PQC project describes a transition under its standards framework in which quantum-vulnerable algorithms are ultimately removed from NIST standards by 2035, with higher-risk systems earlier. NIST IR 8547—the document laying out the proposed transition—is still identified by NIST as an **Initial Public Draft**, not a bespoke compliance deadline for every private SaaS. Your schedule should instead follow your confidentiality lifetime, system exposure, client lifecycles, vendor readiness and any actual contractual/regulatory obligations. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="13"}

## Remaining uncertainty

The biggest unresolved facts are who terminates your TLS, which algorithms/protocol implementations those components currently use, whether the full 20-year retention period also represents a 20-year **confidentiality requirement**, and how long/updateable your deployed software verifiers are. Those facts could move either TLS or update signing substantially higher in the next-quarter backlog.

The final NIST algorithm standards are not the uncertain part: **FIPS 203 → ML-KEM/key establishment; FIPS 204 → ML-DSA/signatures; FIPS 205 → SLH-DSA/signatures.** The uncertainty is the system-level transition around those primitives—protocol support, interoperability, vendor delivery dates and operational migration. NIST's updated 2026 crypto-agility guidance explicitly treats that transition capability as an implementation-environment problem rather than merely an algorithm-selection exercise. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="14"}

For each cryptographic use, record: *What system and data flow is this? What exact protocol and algorithm are used? Where does the public-key operation occur? Which product/library performs it? Who owns the configuration? What keys and certificates are involved, and what are their lifetimes? How long must the protected information remain confidential or the signature remain trustworthy? Which clients/verifiers must interoperate? Is the component internally changeable or vendor-controlled? Is there already ML-KEM, ML-DSA, or SLH-DSA support? Can algorithms be changed through configuration, or will application/protocol changes be required?*

Those fields closely track NIST's definition of a useful cryptographic inventory: algorithms, protocols and services, keys and their lifecycle, certificates, dependent systems, and—particularly relevant here—the data protected by cryptography and whether it is sensitive or long-lived. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

One additional inventory check is easy to overlook: find **public-key cryptography surrounding stored records**, not just the database cipher. If envelope encryption, backup encryption, KMS import, customer-managed keys, or archival processes use RSA/ECC for key transport or wrapping, those are migration dependencies even though the record payload itself may use AES.

### The vendor questions

The most useful question to the TLS/CDN/load-balancer/cloud vendor is not “Do you support PQC?” It is: **Which production product/version supports ML-KEM, through which TLS negotiation mechanism, for which client combinations, and is that support GA, preview, or experimental?** Then establish whether it is hybrid or PQ-only; whether you control enablement; what happens when a client does not support it; what telemetry exposes negotiated key establishment; whether origin connections as well as browser-to-edge connections are protected; and whether a test endpoint exists.

For the update-signing stack, ask whether its signer, HSM/KMS, artifact format, CI/CD tooling, and—most importantly—**deployed verifiers** support FIPS 204 ML-DSA. Ask whether dual-signing or a controlled transition is supported, whether existing clients can receive a verifier update before the classical trust path is retired, and what key-generation/storage/rotation facilities exist. Ask separately about FIPS 205 SLH-DSA rather than treating “PQC signatures” as one interchangeable capability.

Also ask vendors exactly which implementation and validation status they mean by support. The final FIPS publications exist, but the FIPS 203 page currently carries a planning note about an issue intended for correction in a future revision, and FIPS 204 carries a 2026 errata notice. That is a reason to consume maintained implementations and current errata, not to freeze an early implementation copied directly from a specification. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

## Why the 20-year records change the priority

The migration question is not simply “When will quantum computers arrive?” NIST's current migration FAQ says estimates of a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer vary widely, while still recommending preparation now. More importantly for this SaaS, NIST explicitly says an inventory should identify sensitive or long-lived data potentially exposed to harvest-now/decrypt-later risk. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}

That creates a strong planning inference: **a TLS path carrying records whose confidentiality remains material for 20 years deserves attention before a TLS path carrying ephemeral public content**, all else equal. This is a prioritization rule, not a claim that today's traffic has already been compromised or that a CRQC will exist on a particular date.

Software-update signatures have a different time dimension. There is no harvest-and-decrypt issue; instead, the concern is whether deployed systems will continue accepting a quantum-vulnerable signing mechanism far into the future. Consequently, inventorying **verifier upgradeability and trust-root lifetime** is at least as important as selecting ML-DSA.

## Alternatives and failure modes

The most important alternative to “deploy PQC immediately” is **build crypto agility now and deploy each PQ primitive when the surrounding protocol/product ecosystem is production-ready**. NIST defines crypto agility as the ability to replace or adapt cryptographic algorithms in protocols, software, hardware and infrastructure while maintaining operations, and its current CSWP 39 guidance treats that as environment-specific rather than a universal configuration recipe. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"}

Several failure modes are worth avoiding. Do not implement ML-KEM directly in application code when a maintained TLS stack or managed service should own it. Do not confuse post-quantum TLS **key establishment** with post-quantum TLS **certificate signatures**—they are separate pieces. Do not change only the public internet edge while leaving long-lived sensitive traffic on quantum-vulnerable edge-to-origin or service-to-service connections without knowing that fact. Do not switch update signatures until old verifiers can understand the new trust path. And do not treat SLH-DSA as automatically “better” than ML-DSA merely because it has a different foundation; NIST describes ML-DSA as the primary signature standard and SLH-DSA as the alternative based on different mathematics. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"}

## What the first month should conclude

At day 30, success is **not “PQC migration completed.”** Success is knowing exactly where quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography protects 20-year data; knowing who controls each dependency; having firm vendor answers for ML-KEM and ML-DSA; having tested at least one feasible path where support exists; and having a sequenced migration backlog whose first production changes address the most consequential long-lived confidentiality exposure.

I would give **TLS key establishment carrying the 20-year records the first discovery and vendor-testing priority**, followed closely by the software-update signing trust chain. That prioritization comes from the supplied confidentiality horizon plus NIST's risk-oriented inventory guidance; it does **not** imply a universal deadline or a requirement to push immature protocol combinations into production.

NIST does publish transition expectations for its standards: its current PQC project page refers to NIST IR 8547's transition timeline and says high-risk systems should move earlier. But **IR 8547 remains an Initial Public Draft**, and those NIST transition dates should not be converted into an invented blanket deadline for this private SaaS. Your actual production dates depend on data risk, customers/regulation, protocol maturity, client compatibility, and vendor readiness. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

## Resulting question tree

Your immediate question is “what should one engineer do in the next 30 days?”, but the decision depends on several deeper branches:

1. **What cryptographic jobs does the SaaS actually perform?**
   - TLS key establishment protecting customer-record traffic.
   - Authentication/signatures inside TLS and PKI.
   - Software-update/code signatures.
   - Possibly asymmetric key wrapping in KMS/HSMs, backup systems, database encryption, identity, SSH, VPNs, webhooks, package signing, or third-party APIs.
   - Which of these use RSA, Diffie-Hellman/ECDH, ECDSA, EdDSA, or other quantum-vulnerable public-key mechanisms?

2. **Which NIST standards map to those jobs?**
   - Key establishment → FIPS 203 / ML-KEM.
   - Digital signatures → FIPS 204 / ML-DSA, with FIPS 205 / SLH-DSA as a different-family signature alternative.
   - Symmetric encryption is a separate problem; PQC does not mean replacing AES indiscriminately.

3. **What creates urgency?**
   - The 20-year confidentiality requirement creates exposure to “harvest now, decrypt later”: encrypted traffic captured now may remain valuable long enough to attack later.
   - Software-update signatures face a different threat: future ability to forge authentication/integrity evidence.
   - Therefore confidentiality and signing should be inventoried and prioritized separately.

4. **What is actually under your control?**
   - Application code?
   - TLS library?
   - CDN/load balancer/cloud provider?
   - Managed KMS/HSM?
   - Certificate authority?
   - Package/update distribution infrastructure?
   - Client software whose verifier cannot easily be upgraded?

5. **What can reasonably happen with one engineer?**
   - A complete migration is unlikely to be the right 30-day objective.
   - A useful objective is a decision-grade crypto inventory, vendor capability map, prioritized migration backlog, and one bounded interoperability test.

6. **What could reverse the priorities?**
   - Customer records cease being sensitive long before 20 years.
   - TLS is already terminated by infrastructure with a production-supported PQC/hybrid key exchange.
   - An immutable installed client base makes changing update verification much harder than changing server TLS.
   - A critical dependency has no viable PQC migration path.
   - Regulatory/customer obligations impose a more specific timetable than generic NIST guidance.

That leads to the following plan.

---

# A. Direct answer

For this SaaS, **the first 30 days should be a discovery-and-readiness sprint, not a company-wide PQC deployment**.

For the two cryptographic functions you explicitly identified:

| Function | NIST standard | Practical interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| TLS/shared-secret **key establishment** | **FIPS 203 — ML-KEM** | This is the PQC primitive to track for replacing quantum-vulnerable RSA/DH/ECDH-style key-establishment dependencies. A KEM establishes a shared secret that can then be used by symmetric encryption. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"} |
| Software-update **digital signatures** | **FIPS 204 — ML-DSA** | Treat this as the first signature standard to evaluate for ordinary signing deployments; NIST describes ML-DSA as its primary digital-signature standard. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"} |
| Alternative digital signature | **FIPS 205 — SLH-DSA** | Also standardized for signatures, but based on hash functions rather than the lattice construction used by ML-DSA. NIST described it as a backup/diversity option if ML-DSA were compromised. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"} |

All three final FIPS were published **August 13, 2024**. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="3"}

For this particular company, the 20-year retention requirement puts **TLS/key-establishment discovery near the front of the queue**. NIST specifically warns that long-lived secrets create “harvest now, decrypt later” risk: attackers can retain intercepted encrypted material and attempt to decrypt it once sufficiently capable quantum computing exists. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="4"}

That does **not** mean “replace TLS with raw ML-KEM.” FIPS 203 defines a KEM; actual deployment depends on the TLS stack, protocol constructions, cloud/CDN/load-balancer support, clients, and interoperability. NIST's migration project explicitly treats vendor implementation and protocol interoperability as a separate workstream. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="5"}

## A realistic first 30 days

| Period | One-engineer objective | Concrete output |
|---|---|---|
| **Days 1–5** | Define scope and start cryptographic inventory | One spreadsheet/repository listing external TLS endpoints, service-to-service TLS, update-signing pipeline, KMS/HSM use, certificates, libraries, proxies/CDNs and customer-facing clients |
| **Days 6–10** | Discover actual algorithms and dependencies | Record RSA/ECDSA/ECDH/etc., TLS versions, cert chains, crypto libraries, termination points, keys and responsible vendor/service |
| **Days 11–15** | Risk-rank the findings | Separate long-lived-confidentiality systems from signature/authentication systems; identify the traffic carrying records that may remain sensitive for years |
| **Days 16–20** | Get vendor roadmaps | Obtain explicit PQC support, protocol, product-version, interoperability, KMS/HSM and certificate answers from the handful of vendors that control your critical crypto |
| **Days 21–25** | Run one non-production proof | Prefer the highest-value dependency where production-supported PQC or hybrid key establishment already exists; test compatibility, latency/message-size impact, logging and rollback |
| **Days 26–30** | Produce the migration roadmap | Inventory, prioritized blockers, vendor commitments, testing results, next-quarter engineering backlog and explicit triggers for deployment |

The month-one success criterion should therefore be **“we know what must migrate, who controls each dependency, what is available now, and what to test next”**, not “all production traffic and signatures use PQC.”

That approach closely follows NIST NCCoE's migration model: cryptographic discovery/inventory first, then risk-based prioritization and interoperability work. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="6"}

---

# B. Expanded findings

### 1. The inventory is the highest-leverage artifact

NIST's June 2026 migration FAQ defines a cryptographic inventory broadly. It can include algorithms; protocols such as TLS, SSH, VPN and code signing; keys and their lifecycle information; certificates and chains; systems/components dependent on cryptography; and the data being protected—particularly sensitive, long-lived information. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}

For this SaaS, I would make each inventory row contain:

**System/component → cryptographic purpose → protocol → current public-key algorithm → symmetric algorithm where relevant → library/service/provider → key/cert owner → certificate expiration/key lifecycle → data protected → required confidentiality lifetime → externally observable traffic? → client/verifier dependencies → PQC capability → migration blocker → owner.**

Do not store private-key material in that inventory.

This reveals a common blind spot: “we use TLS” is not sufficiently specific. TLS might terminate at a CDN, cloud load balancer, ingress proxy, service mesh, application runtime or appliance. The SaaS may not actually control the cryptographic primitive at the place where migration must occur.

### 2. Give long-lived confidentiality special attention

NIST notes that full integration of new cryptography historically can take **10–20 years**, while the date of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is unknown. More importantly for your case, already-captured encrypted information can remain exposed to later decryption. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="8"}

A useful priority function is therefore roughly:

**confidentiality lifetime × sensitivity × interception exposure × migration lead time.**

Twenty years of record retention is not automatically 20 years of confidentiality. That is one of the first business facts to establish. If individual records remain commercially, legally, or personally sensitive for most of that period, today's externally observable TLS flows deserve more urgency than data whose secrecy loses value after months.

Also inspect **backups and key wrapping**. AES-encrypted data at rest is not equivalent to RSA/ECDH key establishment; however, a symmetric data-encryption key may itself be protected by quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography somewhere in the key-management architecture.

### 3. Software-update signing is important for a different reason

FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 are signature standards: they protect authenticity and detect unauthorized modification. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="9"}

For software updates, the difficult problem is often not generating a PQ signature. It is upgrading the **entire verification trust chain**:

signing system → key storage/HSM → package format → distribution service → certificate/metadata format → installed client's verifier → rollback/recovery procedure.

A server-side TLS upgrade can sometimes be largely vendor-controlled. A signing migration can be harder if old clients contain fixed verification code or trust anchors and must continue accepting updates for years.

Therefore, during the first month, determine the **oldest supported updater/verifier** and whether its signature algorithm is replaceable without physically or operationally stranding it.

### 4. ML-DSA versus SLH-DSA

For an ordinary new update-signing design, investigate **ML-DSA/FIPS 204 first**. NIST explicitly described FIPS 204 as its primary digital-signature standard. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="10"}

SLH-DSA is not “stronger ML-DSA.” It is a separate hash-based construction offering algorithmic diversity. NIST described FIPS 205 as a backup in case ML-DSA proves vulnerable. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="11"}

That diversity matters, but it does not imply a small SaaS should immediately build dual-signature infrastructure. Compatibility, signature sizes, tooling, verification environment and vendor support matter more than choosing two algorithms on paper.

### 5. Crypto agility matters almost as much as the immediate algorithm

NIST defines crypto agility as being able to replace/adapt algorithms in protocols, applications, software, hardware, firmware and infrastructure while maintaining security and operations. Its latest final white paper is CSWP 39upd1, updated June 29, 2026. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="12"}

For a one-engineer team, that suggests avoiding hard-coded crypto choices where an existing library, KMS, TLS stack or platform-supported abstraction can carry the transition.

The strategic question is not only:

> “Can this product support ML-KEM today?”

but also:

> “When its cryptographic recommendation changes again, can we replace it without redesigning the product?”

---

# C. Questions you would probably have asked next

### “What should we ask our TLS/cloud/CDN vendor?”

Ask for specific, verifiable answers:

- Which production product/version supports **NIST-standardized ML-KEM**, and through which TLS or hybrid key-establishment construction?
- Is it generally available or preview/experimental?
- Which client/browser/runtime versions interoperate?
- What happens when the peer lacks PQC support: negotiated fallback, connection failure, or separate endpoint?
- Can you report which connections negotiated PQC versus classical key establishment?
- Does enabling it affect certificate handling, TLS termination topology, packet size, CPU, memory or latency?
- Is the implementation covered by relevant cryptographic validation requirements your customers need?
- What is the vendor's migration/retirement roadmap for RSA/ECDH dependencies?

NIST's migration work specifically stresses interoperability testing because vendors and standards bodies must integrate PQC into real protocols rather than users merely substituting an algorithm. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="13"}

### “What should we ask the code-signing/KMS/HSM vendor?”

Ask:

- Do you support **ML-DSA/FIPS 204** keys and operations?
- Do you support **SLH-DSA/FIPS 205**, and for what use cases?
- Can the existing HSM/KMS generate and retain those private keys?
- Are key import/export, backup, rotation and disaster recovery supported?
- Which signing formats and artifact ecosystems support them?
- Can classical and PQ signatures coexist during a transition?
- What verifier/toolchain versions are required?
- How will existing clients obtain support for the new verification algorithm?
- What is the rollback mechanism if interoperability problems emerge?
- What product/release milestone represents supported production use rather than a demonstration?

### “Should we implement ML-KEM ourselves?”

Generally, **no as a first move**. NIST standardizes the cryptographic primitive, but secure integration into an application or TLS protocol has additional requirements. NIST published final SP 800-227 in September 2025 specifically to give recommendations for secure KEM implementation and use. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="14"}

Use well-supported protocol/library/vendor implementations rather than inventing a proprietary “ML-KEM over TCP” or modifying TLS yourself.

### “Should the engineer spend the month benchmarking algorithms?”

Only after identifying a real deployment path. NIST's project splits **discovery** from **interoperability/benchmarking** for a reason. Benchmarking an isolated ML-KEM implementation tells you little if your CDN, client fleet, CA or signing toolchain cannot yet use it. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="15"}

---

# D. Important things you might not have known to ask

**PQC TLS and PQC certificates are not the same migration.** TLS key establishment, certificate signatures and application signatures are separate crypto functions. A connection can gain quantum-resistant key establishment while other parts of its PKI remain classical during a transition.

**The 20-year number needs semantic clarification.** “Stored for 20 years” does not necessarily mean “must remain secret for 20 years.” The confidentiality lifetime, rather than database retention policy alone, drives harvest-now/decrypt-later priority.

**Third parties may dominate your schedule.** For a SaaS, your cloud provider, TLS terminator, CA, KMS/HSM, language/runtime, update framework and customer client platforms may constrain migration more than your own source code. NIST's migration program explicitly includes hardware, software, services and vendor interoperability. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="16"}

**Parameter-set selection should not be improvised.** FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 with different security/performance properties. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="17"} The first month should discover what the applicable protocol/profile/vendor specifies rather than having one engineer select a parameter set independently.

**Monitor errata.** NIST currently has planning notes for future corrections to FIPS 203 and, as of July 31, 2026, several minor issues for FIPS 204. That is another reason to consume maintained implementations rather than transcribing standards directly into application code. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="18"}

---

# E. Contradictions and alternative explanations

One apparently contradictory recommendation is:

**“Migrate immediately because long-lived data is already at risk”** versus **“do not rush an implementation.”**

Both can be true. NIST says the standardized algorithms can be used now, and it emphasizes the harvest-now/decrypt-later concern. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="19"} But its migration work also emphasizes discovery and interoperability. An unsupported home-built deployment can create new security or availability failures.

The practical interpretation for a one-engineer SaaS is therefore:

**start the migration immediately; do not equate “start” with “force a production cryptographic cutover during month one.”**

A second tension concerns priorities. Long-retention data points toward TLS/key establishment first. But software-update signing could instead become first operationally if compromise of the update channel would give an attacker catastrophic access and the verifier fleet takes years to migrate. Quantum risk is only one part of security risk; your eventual roadmap should combine it with ordinary compromise impact.

A third misconception is that FIPS 203 is simply “the new encryption algorithm.” Its actual standardized role is **key encapsulation/key establishment**. The resulting secret is then used with symmetric cryptography. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="20"}

---

# F. Remaining uncertainties

Several material facts cannot be established from the case description:

- Whether customer records remain confidential for all 20 years.
- Where TLS terminates and which party selects the key-establishment mechanism.
- Which public-key algorithms are currently negotiated.
- Whether browsers, native clients, SDKs or machine-to-machine consumers constrain TLS compatibility.
- Whether the SaaS uses asymmetric cryptography for encryption-at-rest key wrapping.
- Which algorithm currently signs updates.
- Whether old update clients can receive a verifier capable of ML-DSA/SLH-DSA.
- Whether the signing key resides in an HSM/KMS and whether that product supports PQC.
- Whether customer contracts, regulated-data obligations or government procurement requirements impose a separate timetable.

There is also no exact date at which a cryptographically relevant quantum computer will exist; NIST explicitly says that date is unknown. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="21"}

NIST's **IR 8547** does contain proposed transition timelines for quantum-vulnerable algorithms, but as of September 2026 the official NIST page still labels IR 8547 an **Initial Public Draft**, not a final standard. It is intended to inform agencies, industry and standards organizations, not to establish one universal deployment deadline for every private SaaS. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="22"}

So I would **not convert its dates into “your SaaS must be PQC-complete by X.”**

---

# G. Information that would most change the conclusion

The seven highest-value facts to collect during week one are:

1. **Actual secrecy lifetime of customer records**, not merely retention duration.
2. **TLS termination architecture** and responsible vendors.
3. **Current TLS key-establishment/signature algorithms** on every externally reachable path.
4. **Installed-client population and upgradeability**, particularly any long-lived agents or desktop/mobile software.
5. **Current update-signing algorithm, key store and verification chain.**
6. **PQC roadmaps/support status from the TLS, cloud, CA and KMS/HSM providers.**
7. **Contractual/regulatory deadlines or customers requiring NIST/FIPS-aligned migration.**

If those answers show that your cloud/TLS provider already offers a supported interoperable PQC key-establishment path, the next-quarter plan could include a staged production rollout. If instead support is missing in a key client, HSM or certificate/signing ecosystem, the correct near-term outcome is a dependency-management roadmap rather than custom cryptographic engineering.

**Root decision:** With one engineer, what should this SaaS do in the next 30 days to reduce post-quantum risk without attempting a premature, incompatible crypto rewrite?

1. **What is actually exposed to quantum risk?**

6. **Should you wait for more PQC standards?**  
   - NIST has selected HQC as a future second KEM, but ML-KEM is already finalized.  
   - Additional signature work continues. Does waiting reduce risk, or merely prolong exposure and migration debt?

7. **What deadline actually applies?**
